note: clay test scene: grey materials only, so the diagrams show exactly what each pass does to the light. same screen-space maths ReShade runs on the game.

slides.title: full preset
slides.text: every pass stacked in order: occlusion, light scattering, bloom, depth of field, then the grade. ReShade runs this after the game draws each frame, reading the game's own depth buffer.

slides.title: light scattering
slides.text: bright sky around the sun is isolated using depth, then every pixel samples 120 times along a line toward the sun. palms, poles and buildings block samples, and those gaps become rays.

slides.title: ambient occlusion
slides.text: 24 points in a hemisphere around each surface are tested against depth. corners, contact points and creases that can't see the open sky get darker, so objects sit in the world instead of floating.

slides.title: depth of field
slides.text: distance from the focus plane sets each pixel's blur radius. samples closer than the pixel are weighted down, so sharp foreground edges don't smear into the background.

slides.title: bloom
slides.text: only light above a brightness threshold is kept: the lamps and the sun's core. it's blurred at three sizes and added back, the way a real lens glows.

slides.title: colour grading
slides.text: the HDR frame is tonemapped with the ACES filmic curve, then the look is applied: lifted blacks and a gentle S-curve. the whole grade is one curve from light in to pixel out, which ReShade stores as a small lookup texture.
